arguments.claim: The Government argued that the trial court’s decision to have the four witnesses examined by the courts of their places of residence pursuant to letters of request sent to those courts had been taken in accordance with Article 180 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided for such a method under certain circumstances.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court's interpretation and application of Article 180 as an inflexible and mechanical approach that did not constitute a good reason for non-attendance of witnesses.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that Y.A., S.Y. and A.T. were all convicted persons serving prison sentences in different cities, and that F.K. could not be located despite efforts.

anchor.surface_text: 42.�Y.A., S.Y. and A.T. were all convicted persons who had been serving prison sentences in three different cities in Turkey. As for F.K., the trial court had revoked its decision to take evidence from him after efforts to locate him had been to no avail.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted that the fact that witnesses were in prison did not by itself constitute a good reason for their non-attendance and that the efforts to locate F.K. were insufficient.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the applicant’s lawyer had been notified of the hearings held in the courts which had taken evidence from those witnesses, but had not attended any of the commission hearings.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the absence of the lawyer at commission hearings was not a sufficient procedural safeguard given the lack of good reason for witness non-attendance.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the trial court had carried out a meticulous assessment of the evidence in the case file before convicting the applicant and had not found credible the evidence given by the witnesses before the courts acting on the letters of request, setting out reasons to attach more weight to their initial statements.

anchor.surface_text: 43.�Moreover, the trial court had carried out a meticulous assessment of the evidence in the case file before convicting the applicant. In that connection, it had not found credible the evidence given by the witnesses before the courts acting on the letters of request, setting out the reasons leading it to attach more weight to their initial statements.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court observed that the trial court did not approach the evidence given by absent witnesses with particular caution or awareness of its reduced weight due to their absence.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the trial court had provided a reasoned reply to the applicant’s allegations that there had been more than one person with the code name “Avareş”.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the trial court did not address the question whether the persons named 'Avareş' were the same or different, which was significant given the identification issues.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the inability to confront witnesses in person without good reason and reliance on their evidence tainted the fairness of the proceedings.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court’s interpretation and application of Article 180 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, resulting in witnesses always being examined by courts of their places of residence if residing elsewhere, was an inflexible and mechanical approach that could not be considered a good reason for non-attendance at trial.

anchor.surface_text: 55.�When viewed in the light of the above principles, the Court notes that the interpretation and application of Article 180 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the trial court meant that the witnesses would always be examined by the courts of their places of residence if they were residing in a city other than where the trial was taking place.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that this approach precludes individualised assessment and absolves courts of their duty to secure witness attendance, thus not a good reason.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the fact that three witnesses were serving sentences in prisons under State control did not prompt the trial court to assess whether it was possible to hear them in person, which was a failure.

anchor.surface_text: 56.�Indeed, the fact that three of the witnesses were serving their sentences in different prisons in Turkey at the time they gave evidence during the applicant’s trial, and were hence under the exclusive authority of the State, did not prompt the trial court to assess whether it was possible to hear them in person.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court failed to make reasonable efforts to secure attendance despite control over witnesses.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the steps taken to locate F.K. were insufficient and did not suggest that everything reasonably expected was done to secure his presence.

anchor.surface_text: 57.�Similarly, the Court finds that the steps taken by the domestic authorities to locate F.K., which consisted only of enquiring at his alleged work address and calling a mobile telephone number belonging to him do not suggest that they did everything reasonably expected of them to secure his presence.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that minimal efforts to locate a witness do not meet the obligation to secure attendance.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the evidence given by the four absent witnesses was central and decisive to the applicant’s conviction and that none of the remaining evidence could have been sufficient of itself to find the applicant guilty.

anchor.surface_text: 60.�While it is true that the trial court had in its possession the statements made by other witnesses and incident reports regarding the acts attributed to the applicant, it appears from the trial court’s reasoned judgment that the evidence given by the four absent witnesses was central to his conviction given that none of the remaining evidence could have been sufficient of itself to find the applicant guilty.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the conviction relied decisively on absent witnesses' evidence.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court failed to explore alternative measures for obtaining evidence from the absent witnesses as required by Article 180 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, including audiovisual means.

anchor.surface_text: 67.�In that connection, the Court further observes that the second paragraph of Article 180 provides that the examination of witnesses by the courts of their places of residence is only possible if it is difficult to bring them before the trial court. However, the trial court’s decision was silent on this crucial requirement. Similarly, while the fifth paragraph of the same provision stipulates that wherever possible the courts should have recourse to audiovisual means of taking statements from witnesses who reside outside their jurisdiction, the trial court does not appear to have considered that method either.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court did not consider alternative methods or provide reasons for not doing so.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the method of examining witnesses by courts of their places of residence was not capable of allowing the defence to properly and fairly assess the credibility of the evidence, especially given the burden on the defence and the applicant's detention.

anchor.surface_text: 68.�Be that as it may, in order to consider the first limb of the Government’s argument, the Court ought also to examine the preliminary question of whether the method the trial court opted for, namely issuing letters of request to the courts of the absent witnesses’ places of residence to take evidence from them, was such as to allow the defence to properly and fairly assess the credibility of the evidence. The Court is unable to answer that question in the affirmative in the present case for the following reasons.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that the method imposed disproportionate burdens and did not allow proper assessment of evidence credibility.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the theoretical possibility for the applicant’s lawyer to attend hearings in different cities did not constitute a sufficient counterbalancing factor to compensate for the absence of witnesses at trial.

anchor.surface_text: 71.�Accordingly, the Court concludes that the hearing of witnesses by the courts of their places of residence is not capable of operating as a procedural safeguard in the absence of good reasons for the non-attendance of absent witnesses and when the trial court had recourse to it without considering alternative measures for obtaining evidence from the absent witnesses.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that this approach would undermine the principle that evidence must normally be produced in the accused's presence.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court did not approach the evidence given by the absent witnesses with particular caution or awareness of its reduced weight due to their absence from the trial.

anchor.surface_text: 72.�As regards the second limb of the Government’s argument, the Court observes that there is no indication in the case file that the national courts either approached the evidence given by the absent witnesses with any particular caution or that they were aware that it carried less weight owing to their absence from the trial.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the absence of caution or awareness of reduced evidential weight by the trial court.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court disregarded inconsistencies in witness statements, such as A.T.'s statement that 'Avareş' had been arrested, which was crucial and exemplified the need to hear witnesses in person.

anchor.surface_text: 73.�Moreover, the Court observes that the trial court concluded that the description given by A.T. in 1999 of the organisation member with the code name “Avareş” who had lines on his face perfectly matched that of the applicant, given that he also had lines on his face. Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that the trial court simply disregarded the fact that A.T. had also stated in 1999 that “Avareş” had been arrested.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that disregarding such inconsistencies undermined the reliability assessment of evidence.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the applicant’s conviction rested on the untested evidence of absent witnesses whom he had no real opportunity to examine either when they made their statements or during the criminal proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: 74.�Given the above shortcomings, and reiterating that the assessment of the trustworthiness of a witness is a task which usually cannot be achieved by a mere reading of his or her recorded words, the Court takes the view that the examination carried out by the trial court was not, by and of itself, such as to counteract the adverse impact that the admission of the evidence given by the absent witnesses had on the fairness of the criminal proceedings against the applicant.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded that the lack of opportunity to examine witnesses tainted the fairness of the proceedings.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the four witnesses’ non-attendance at trial, the lack of an in-person confrontation without good reason, and reliance on their evidence by the trial court without necessary procedural safeguards, substantially affected the defence’s ability to test the evidence and tainted the overall fairness of the proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: 75.�Accordingly, the four witnesses’ non-attendance at trial, the lack of an in-person confrontation between them and the applicant without a good reason and the reliance placed upon their evidence by the trial court in convicting the applicant and sentencing him to life imprisonment without the necessary procedural safeguards, substantially affected the defence’s ability to test the truthfulness and reliability of their evidence and, in the circumstances of the present case, tainted the overall fairness of the proceedings against the applicant.
